newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria adopts election law, preparing for poll.
newsitem.headline: Algeria adopts election law, preparing for poll.

text.p: Algeria's government-appointed Transitional National Council (CNT) on Wednesday passed into law a new voting system based on proportional representation, Algerian state-run radio said.
The law is seen as a new obstacle aimed at preventing legal Islamists from dominating a new parliament due to be chosen in a general election in the first half of this year.

Algeria has been without a parliament since January 1992 when the authorities scrapped an election in which the now outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) took a commanding lead under a straight majority-system vote.
Scrapping the ballot plunged Algeria into violence in which about 60,000 people have died in the past five years.
The authorities appointed the CNT in place of the parliament to enable the government to adopt legislation.

President Liamine Zeroual has ruled out involvement of the FIS in the elections but political sources said the government and secular opposition leaders fear the legal fundamentalist Hamas party may take its place in dominating the poll.
The elections are planned to be held between May 29 and June 5.
The law gives Hamas and Nahda, a second legal fundamentalist party, two months to change their manifestos to avoid running foul of the legislation, political sources said.
Hamas leader Mahfoud Nahnah gained one third of the vote in the 1995 plural presidential election which returned Zeroual to power.

The law sets the number of deputies in the national assembly -- the lower house -- at 380. It gives women a greater opportunity to stand for election by exempting them from having to prove a minimum level of support in the constituency they hope to represent.
Under the Algerian constitution, adopted last November, the national assembly and the National Council (upper house) will form the new parliament.

Two thirds of the National Council's 144 members will be picked by the elected local authorities while the other third will be selected by the president from the ranks of leading personalities, union officials and other professionals.
The CNT on Tuesday voted a party law that bans political parties from having a platform based on Islam, language, regionalism or gender.
Both laws are widely seen as part of an attempt by Zeroual's government to realign the political field after Algeria's failed bid to establish a democracy in the early 1990s.

Many Algerians blame the current bloody struggle over power on a previous law that allowed the FIS to enter politics. That law ushered in the start of Algeria's democratic experiment in 1989, and produced more than 60 political parties competing for power.

The new party law also stipulates that every party should be able to show it has a minimum of 2,500 supporters spread over at least 25 of the country's 48 provinces. Some politicians say this will mean the end of many parties.
